```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(lubridate)
library(validate)
library(testthat)
library(here)
```
```{r}
# Reading in my data
strava <- read_csv(
  here("Strava Analysis", "data", "activities.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```
```{r}
# Examine the dimensions of the original dataset
dim(strava)

# Examine variables only relevant to the research question
strava |>
  select(
    `Activity Date`,
    `Activity Type`,
    `Distance...7`,
    `Distance...18`,
    `Moving Time`
  ) |>
  glimpse()
```
This dataset consists of my personal Strava activity records. I obtained the data by exporting my activity history from Strava. I examined the dataset’s dimensions, variable types, and column names to identify any inconsistencies

# Data Cleaning

To prepare my Strava data for analysis, I standardized the column names using clean_names() and identified duplicate distance variables recorded in different units. I selected the distance variable measured in metres and converted it to kilometres. I  filtered the dataset to include only running activities. This reduced the observations from 165 to 114. I also converted moving time from seconds to minutes, so average pace was calculated in minutes per kilometre. Lastly, I formatted activity dates, extracted the year, and categorized runs as short-distance (≤5 miles) or long-distance (>5 miles) to examine changes in running performance over time.
```{r}
# Standardize column names
strava_clean <- strava |>
  clean_names()
```
```{r}
# Examine the different activity types in the original dataset
strava_clean |>
  count(activity_type, sort = TRUE)
```
I examined the distribution of activity types before filtering the dataset. Because the research question focuses specifically on running pace, I kept only activities classified as "Run." Other activity types were left out of the analytical dataset.

Now lets look at our relevant columns!
```{r}
strava_clean |>
  select(
    activity_type,
    activity_date,
    distance_7,
    distance_18,
    moving_time
  ) |>
  head(10)
```
```{r}
# Prepare the dataset for analysis
strava_runs <- strava_clean |>

  # Retain only running activities
  filter(activity_type == "Run") |>

  mutate(

    # Convert distance from metres to kilometres
    distance_km = as.numeric(distance_18) / 1000,

    # Convert moving time from seconds to minutes
    moving_time_min = as.numeric(moving_time) / 60,

    # Convert activity dates and extract the year
    activity_date = mdy_hms(activity_date, quiet = TRUE),
    year = year(activity_date),

    # Calculate average running pace in minutes per kilometre
    pace_min_km = if_else(
      distance_km > 0,
      moving_time_min / distance_km,
      NA_real_
    ),

    # Categorize runs based on a five-mile threshold
    distance_category = case_when(
      distance_km <= 8.04672 ~ "Short Distance",
      distance_km > 8.04672 ~ "Long Distance",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
 
```

# Meaningful Tests

## Test 1: Check whether distances and moving times are valid

```{r}
rules <- validator(
  distance_km > 0,
  moving_time_min > 0,
  !is.na(distance_km),
  !is.na(moving_time_min)
)

validation_results <- confront(strava_runs, rules)

summary(validation_results)
```
## Test 2: Check whether cleaning preserved the number of running activities
```{r}
original_runs <- strava_clean |>
  filter(activity_type == "Run")

test_that("Cleaning preserves the number of running activities", {

  expect_equal(
    nrow(original_runs),
    nrow(strava_runs)
  )

})
```

## Test 3: Verify the pace calculation

```{r}
test_that("Running pace is calculated correctly", {

  valid_runs <- strava_runs |>
    filter(
      !is.na(distance_km),
      !is.na(moving_time_min),
      distance_km > 0
    )

  expect_equal(
    valid_runs$pace_min_km,
    valid_runs$moving_time_min / valid_runs$distance_km
  )

})
```

## Test 4: Check that activity dates were converted correctly

```{r}
test_that("All running activity dates are valid", {

  expect_false(
    any(is.na(strava_runs$activity_date))
  )

})
```

## Test 5: Check for dupilicate activities

```{r}
test_that("Running activities have unique IDs", {

  expect_equal(
    n_distinct(strava_runs$activity_id),
    nrow(strava_runs)
  )

})
```

I conducted several tests to assess the quality and consistency of my cleaned Strava data. All tests passed. This confirms that running distances and moving times were positive and contained no missing values, activity dates were successfully converted, and no duplicate activity IDs were identified. I also verified that the cleaning process preserved the number of running activities and that average pace was calculated consistently.

# Exploratory analysis

## Graph 1: Distribution of running distances

```{r}
strava_runs |>
  ggplot(aes(x = distance_km)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "steelblue",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Running Distances",
    x = "Distance (km)",
    y = "Number of Runs"
  )
```

This histogram shows that my running activities are concentrated around certain distances, particularly shorter and mid-range runs. This suggests that my running routine involves frequently repeated distances rather than an even distribution. As seen in the data, I frequently do 3.3 km (or 2 mile) runs.

```{r}
# Count the number of recorded runs per year
strava_runs |>
  filter(year >= 2023, year <= 2026) |>
  count(year, name = "number_of_runs")
```
Before examining changes in running pace, I looked at the number of activities recorded each year. Interestingly, I recorded the most runs in 2023, with the number of recorded activities decreasing in subsequent years
  

## Graph 2: The relationship between distance and pace

```{r}
strava_runs |>
  filter(
    year >= 2023,
    year <= 2026,
    is.finite(pace_min_km)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = activity_date,
      y = pace_min_km
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.5,
    colour = "steelblue"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "darkred"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Changes in Running Pace, 2023–2026",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Average Pace (min/km)"
  )
```
The scatterplot reveals a downward trend in average running pace between 2023 and 2026, suggesting that my running speed has generally improved over time. Since lower values in minutes per kilometre indicate faster running, the negative slope represents an improvement in pace. Interestingly, it looks like the observations become less dispersed over time. This suggests an increase in consistency in my running performance. 

## Graph 3: Running pace by distance category

```{r}
strava_runs |>
  filter(
    year >= 2023,
    year <= 2026,
    is.finite(pace_min_km),
    !is.na(distance_category)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = factor(year),
      y = pace_min_km,
      fill = distance_category
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Running Pace by Year and Distance Category",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Pace (min/km)",
    fill = "Distance Category"
  )
```
The boxplots suggest that my average running pace has generally improved across both short- and long-distance activities between 2023 and 2026. The data also appear to show greater variation in pace during earlier years, especially 2023. However, differences in the number of recorded runs across years and distance categories may influence these patterns. For instance, in 2023, I was training for a longer-distance event, which meant that I completed longer runs more frequently. The increased training volume and potentially limited recovery time may have contributed to slower recorded paces. In subsequent years, I shifted toward shorter distances because I found them more enjoyable. It is possible that both the shorter distances and greater enjoyment of these activities influenced my running pace. This change in training preferences provides important context for interpreting the observed patterns, as differences in pace may reflect changes in my running goals and motivation rather than improvements in physical performance alone.

## Graph 4: Distance and pace

```{r}
strava_runs |>
  filter(
    is.finite(pace_min_km)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = distance_km,
      y = pace_min_km
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.6,
    colour = "steelblue"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "darkred"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Running Distance and Pace",
    x = "Distance (km)",
    y = "Average Pace (min/km)"
  )
```
The scatterplot suggests a weak positive relationship between running distance and average pace, indicating that longer runs tend to be completed at slightly slower speeds. However, I wonder if this relationship may reflect differences in training purpose rather than distance alone. For example, longer runs are intended to build endurance, whereas shorter runs may be completed at higher intensities. The presence of several extreme pace observations, particularly among shorter distances. This suggests that running distance alone does not adequately explain variations in my performance. This raises questions about how factors such as training goals, fatigue, and motivation influence running pace, none of which are directly captured in the dataset.

# Reflection

Something I found interesting, maybe not surprising, was how my running pace became faster and more consistent over time, despite running less frequently. In 2023, I recorded more runs than in any other year, yet my average pace was slower and much less consistent. As the years progressed, I recorded fewer runs, but my pace generally improved. Initially, I found this somewhat counterintuitive because I assumed that running more frequently would lead to better performance. However, reflecting on my training habits, I wonder if this could be related to having more recovery time, incorporating more weightlifting between runs, and shifting toward shorter distances. Although I cannot determine exactly what caused these changes from my data, I think it's interesting that running less frequently coincided with faster and more consistent paces.
